notes.1a: Candidates were able to identify key definitions of a species, such as individuals breeding together to produce fertile offspring, but many candidates lost credit because they did not give any detail of the features, i.e. they did not state morphological, physiological, etc.
notes.1b: The most common problem here was giving allopatric speciation as an answer; ‘allopatric speciation’ is a term which implies geographical isolation, but does not explain how separation has been physically caused.
notes.1c: Most candidates were awarded some credit here. It was obvious when candidates had learnt by rote the answer to this question, and perhaps had looked at past exam questions in order to identify key marking points for this style of question. Allopatric speciation was used in responses and described clearly. There were very few candidates who discussed the idea of the mating song not being recognised by the females, but good coverage of all other marking points. notes.2i: This was a difficult question, not least because the graph required a lot of interpretation. Candidates would be well advised to make sure in descriptions of data that they clearly identify the trend. A common reason for not scoring marks here was incorrect reading of the results from the graph; group P is quite clearly 30.5% and not, for example, 30%. Many candidates stated that results in groups S and T were different; a 0.5% difference should not be considered meaningfully different. A proportion of the candidates simply wrote out the data in the graph but did not interpret in any way.
notes.2ii: Very few candidates were awarded credit for this question. Perhaps most candidates do not consider 71 people to be a small number, but in the context of this kind of investigation it is a small
notes.2iii: Candidates struggled here; many seemed to understand the concept and knew that plasma cells cannot divide or grow in culture. They stated that myeloma cells will divide but did not specify indefinitely or continuously.
notes.2iv: Some candidates talked about markers, but did not qualify properly what the marker could have been attached to. Simply adding antigens to the solution would not identify hybridoma cells. Very few candidates suggested the use of labelled antigens or gave valid methods of marking or identifying the antigen. A small number gave other valid methods of identifying the hybridoma
notes.2c: A commonly given response was that monoclonal antibodies give a faster diagnosis, but many other points given referred to treatment, despite diagnosis being emphasised in the question.
notes.3a: Many candidates were unclear about this topic. They knew the movement of DNA to the anode, but failed to say that it was the phosphate group of the DNA that was negatively charged. Those who attempted to describe that lower mass moved faster were awarded, but candidates who wrote about the distance moved needed to include ‘per unit time’.
notes.3b: Candidates generally drew a band in the same place as the band for the HbA HbA individual, but did not correctly draw the second band above it.
notes.3c: Many candidates referred to checking family histories but did not give enough detail. A few mentioned genetic counselling. Many incorrect answers gave information concerning paternity testing and use in criminal investigations.

notes.4i: Many candidates were confused by the data and a fair number did not provide an answer at all. Mixing was identified but this was sometimes confused by also talking about mating. Some picked up on the variation in the results, and some noticed the discrepancy between males and females. Candidates tended to interpret the data in terms of missing (non-recaptured) borers having moved to other fields, rather than new
notes.4unmarked: borers having come from other fields.
notes.4ii: Candidates did not understand the impact of the strategy and what would be needed for it to be effective. Figures were quoted, but these did not relate to points being made and inbreeding occurring. The credit was mostly awarded for marked females mating with marked males or marked females mating with unmarked males.
notes.5a: Candidates knew the role of progesterone and answers were detailed. Common errors were to references to the uterus wall instead of the lining, and to implantation of the egg or ovum.
notes.5i: Many candidates did not read to the smallest square of the graph and rounded their answer up to 33. Many missed the unit
notes.5days: and a few gave an incorrect unit, e.g. years.
notes.5ii: This was a difficult graph to interpret, but as with other questions, candidates should be encouraged to identify trends; many simply described each curve without using the data to answer the question. Many candidates stated that the different diets caused the rats to reach puberty, without giving any time span; they all reached puberty, so time was needed to make a comparison. As with any graph, there were a number of candidates who describe the y-axis variable affecting the x-axis variable, instead of the correct way around.
notes.6a: Candidates identified the reasons covering a range of marking points for species becoming endangered. They were also able to make links between pollination and a removal of flies.
notes.6i: There was a lot of variation in the answers about the definition of the term biodiversity, but most candidates had learnt the definition and so gained credit here.

notes.7a: Many candidates wrote that the allele symbols were R and r, and then went on to carry out the cross perfectly, using the X and Y chromosome symbols in all genotypes in addition to the colour alleles. Common candidate errors included a number who did not include X and Y at all and scored no credit, or put superscripts on the Y chromosome. Most candidates were quite successful on this question.
notes.7i: Candidates who were not awarded credit here pointed out that the son could only inherit the allele from the mother, but this was not really answering the question. Therefore, although they had scientific knowledge, they were not applying it tightly enough within the given context.
notes.7ii: Many candidates spoiled their answer of ‘heterozygous’ by adding dominant or recessive, however, many were awarded credit.
notes.7iii: There were many candidates whose answer ‘mutation’ did not score because more detail was required; they had not specified gene or allele mutation.
notes.8i: Most candidates completed the table correctly.
notes.8ii: The graph was successfully completed by a majority of candidates. Those who did not score full credit made the usual mistakes. These included the axes being the wrong way around, the scales being incorrect, the units missing, points plotted incorrectly and a poorly drawn line.
notes.8iii: The definition of a limiting factor is always something candidates find difficult to explain. When a process is affected by more than one factor, the rate of the reaction is restricted by the factor that is nearest its lowest value. Section B
notes.9a: The question asked the candidates to describe how ATP is synthesised by oxidative phosphorylation. There was some confusion between NADH and NADPH and many missed out the hydrogen being released from the reduced NAD. Electrons accepted by ETC were mentioned, but no mention was made of carriers/cytochromes. Some candidates thought that it was hydrogen that moved rather than the hydrogen ion. Many candidates scored full credit here.
notes.9b: Another well answered question. The need for energy in living organisms was well known and examples were also given. Some missed the reference to light energy in photosynthesis and detail of the light dependent and light independent stages. All other energy requiring processes were well documented.
notes.10a: Candidates were mostly well-prepared and in a few sentences or on a diagram were able to list at least six parts of the kidney. The only thing they were not used to doing was specifying which parts of the nephron were in the cortex and which in the medulla. Where diagrams were used they were used well, with correct labels and the position of nephron identified. Few candidates referred to the afferent and efferent arterioles or the capillary network.
notes.10b: Responses here were very varied from candidates who had shown a thorough knowledge of the functioning of the nephron. Many candidates gave a full account of ultrafiltration and then went on to reabsorption. There was confusion over where the sodium ions were moving from and to. Many gave a muddled account of the facilitated diffusion and cotransporters. Few mentioned osmosis. In the adaptations it was rare to see anything more than microvilli and many mitochondria.
notes.key_messages: ● Candidates should always include units when they give data quotes and copy them correctly from graphs and tables ● Comparative words should be included where appropriate. For example, ‘the electron microscope has a higher resolution than the light microscope’ is preferable to writing ‘the electron microscope has a high resolution’. ● Candidates should read through the entire question before beginning their written response. notes.general_comments: General comments There was a very good spread of scores. Nine questions were answered correctly by more than 75%, Questions 2, 3, 5, 11, 12, 14, 18, 25 and 38. Questions 9, 29, 31, 35 and 39 proved to be more difficult, with fewer than half of the candidates answering them correctly. Comments on specific questions More than half of the candidates answered this correctly, although a significant number of less able candidates thought that starch grains were not visible in a suitable stained plant cell. Candidates who had carried out practical microscopy were more likely to answer correctly.
